title: Scorching Heat Dome Tests World Cup: How FIFA and Host Cities Are Responding
summary:
As a brutal heat dome settles over the U.S. and Canada, the 2026 FIFA World Cup is colliding with one of the hottest weeks of the year—and the consequences are already being felt. In Toronto, health authorities urged fans heading to Thursday’s Portugal-Croatia match to stay hydrated and limit alcohol after Environment Canada issued a heat warning. On Friday, Colombia and Ghana will face off in Kansas City under an extreme heat warning, with “feels like” temperatures reaching a blistering 43°C (110°F). Miami, Philadelphia, and other venues are also bracing for dangerous conditions.

The infrastructure gap between stadiums is stark. Atlanta, Dallas, and Houston boast retractable roofs and air conditioning, offering a climate-controlled bubble once inside. But Toronto’s expanded stadium has only limited roof cover, leaving roughly 43,000 spectators exposed to direct sun. Philadelphia and Kansas City, with capacities near 68,000 and 69,000, similarly lack built-in climate control. Organizers will provide misting stations, cooling zones, and shade, but that may not be enough. Even at indoor venues, the journey to the stadium poses risks: in Dallas, meteorologists warn that pavement temperatures could hit 50°C (122°F), far hotter than the air temperature, because concrete absorbs and radiates heat.

For players, the dangers are severe. Exertional heat stroke—a medical emergency and the third-leading cause of death in athletes—is a real threat. Heat illness can cause dehydration, dizziness, cramping, and extreme fatigue. The game itself changes: players sprint less and conserve energy, altering the pace. FIFA has mandated two three-minute hydration breaks per match, around the midway point of each half, regardless of weather or venue. The policy has drawn criticism from fans and coaches who say it disrupts flow and serves as a commercial opportunity for broadcasters. FIFA President Gianni Infantino pushed back, insisting “the main reason is the heat” and that the organization gains “absolutely nothing” from the breaks.

Other measures include allowing up to five substitutions, at least three rest days between matches, and climate-controlled benches for staff and substitutes at outdoor stadiums. FIFA says it strategically limited outdoor matches during peak heat, adjusted kick-off times, and prioritized covered stadiums for warmer windows. But with temperatures soaring and knockout matches underway, the tournament is a high-stakes test of preparation versus a relentless climate reality.
why_it_matters: As climate change fuels more extreme heat waves, how FIFA protects fans and athletes at outdoor mega-events could set a precedent for everything from Olympic Games to local school sports tournaments in the future.

background_read: The 2026 FIFA World Cup is the first men's World Cup to be hosted across three nations—the United States, Canada, and Mexico—and features 48 teams for the first time, up from 32.
Heat domes occur when a high-pressure system traps hot air like a lid; a similar event in 2021 caused temperatures of nearly 50°C in British Columbia, killing over 600 people.
Gianni Infantino has been FIFA's president since 2016 and has faced criticism over scheduling, but he insists player safety during extreme weather is the top priority.
Environment Canada, the country's national weather and environmental agency, issues heat warnings when humidex values exceed 40°C, indicating a high risk of heat illness.

perspectives.description: FIFA and host cities are taking serious measures—hydration breaks, cooling zones, and climate-controlled benches—to protect players and spectators. These steps can reduce heat-related illness and show that large tournaments can adapt to dangerous conditions.

Critics argue that mandated hydration breaks spoil the flow of the game and give broadcasters extra commercial time, while many fans sit in open-air stadiums with no real cooling. The infrastructure gap means safety is not equal for everyone.

The uneven preparedness of host cities reflects a broader pattern: climate change is making heat waves more intense, but older stadiums were not designed for today's extremes. This mismatch between facilities and weather is a growing problem for global sports.

Future World Cups and outdoor events may need to schedule matches in cooler months or invest in stadiums with roofs and cooling systems. Heat policies like hydration breaks could become standard, and player safety research might change how football is played in hot conditions.
